structured_output.summary:
I searched for evidence on the open hypotheses, with most weight on the stem/BN, Muon-cost, batch-size and averaging branches. Six findings matter most.

1. **H1.3.6 premise confirmed in code.** airbench96_faster's LookaheadState clones the full state_dict. On every update it lerps and copies back every float tensor, BN running_mean and running_var included. The final BN stats are therefore an average over different fast weights, never recomputed for the averaged weights. Wu & Johnson's PreciseBN study found that EMA statistics lag when weights change fast, at high LR or with few updates. In that study, 10^3–10^4 samples were enough for stable stats. H1.3.6 (and H2.3.3) is the cheapest well-grounded test left, at under 0.1 s.

2. **Muon cost (H1.2.3, H1.5.4).** airbench94_muon uses only 3 Newton-Schulz steps (coefficients 3.4445, −4.7750, 2.0315, in bf16). It also renormalizes every filter on every step (`p.data.mul_(len(p)**0.5/p.norm())`), which makes filter weight decay inert. Hiverge also uses 3 NS steps, but renormalizes only every 2 + int(15·progress) steps and shrinks a target norm from 0.50 to 0.079. Two recent papers report that training quality is not monotonic in how exactly the update is orthogonalized: "How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need?" and Polar Express. If the port uses 5 NS steps, dropping to 3 is supported by both reference recipes. If it already uses 3, cheaper per-step options are a 2-step Polar Express variant or less frequent renormalization.

3. **Batch size (H5).** Hiverge's CIFAR-10 record uses batch 1536 under Muon with 7.65 epochs. arXiv 2507.01598 finds Muon needs fewer steps than SGD or AdamW at every batch size tested, on CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 and CIFAR-100 VGG-16. So the claim that Muon tolerates batch changes has some support, but no paper gives a CIFAR-100 optimum near 2000. Seesaw (2510.14717) adds an untested idea: replace part of the late LR decay with a growing batch (LR cut by √α, batch raised by α), which cuts serial steps by up to ~36%. Here it would only save per-step overhead (~5% fixed cost plus ~3.8% Muon NS), and it fails above the critical batch size.

4. **Hiverge settings not yet tried here.** Label smoothing 0.09 (vs 0.3 here), brightness/contrast jitter (0.14/0.13), SGD momentum 0.825, BN momentum 0.5566 with eps 1e-12, and whitening bias trained for 20% of steps (already adopted in E036). Hiverge's record also relies on TTA, which this task bans, so its label-smoothing and jitter values may not transfer.

5. **Stem freezing (H2.6).** FreezeOut reports about 20% less wall-clock time with no accuracy loss for ResNets on CIFAR. MosaicML's layer-freezing write-up reports mixed results elsewhere. This fits E028/E036 and E037's dose limit.

6. **Public CIFAR-100 results and caveats.** The only public competition result is the futurebiohackers PR: 75.29% ±0.25 pp over 40 trials in 8.11 s on an A100-SXM4. The current tip (~5.3 s) is already well ahead of it. airbench96 on CIFAR-100 was run with untuned CIFAR-10 hyperparameters and reports +1.7% over ResNet-18; the search snippet gives no absolute accuracy. Fulcrum's write-up on Fable lists the specification-gaming patterns to avoid: precomputing augmentation in untimed setup, moving whitening into setup, cooldowns and host selection.

Nothing found directly tests H6 (profiler-level kernel efficiency).

findings.claim: LookaheadState clones net.state_dict(). Its update runs ema.lerp_(net, 1-decay) then net.copy_(ema) for every float or half entry, so BN running_mean and running_var are averaged and reset along with the weights. There is no BN recalibration step after training.
findings.relevance: Confirms the premise of H1.3.6 and H2.3.3: the final BN stats are a lerped mixture taken under different fast weights, not stats of the averaged weights. It also means the reset copies BN buffers back too, which bears on the Switch-EMA reading of the reset under H1.3.

findings.claim: Rethinking 'Batch' in BatchNorm (Wu & Johnson). EMA running stats lag behind the model when features change fast (large LR, few updates). In large-batch, short ImageNet training, PreciseBN with 10^4 samples cut error from 52.8% to 39.42% at epoch 30. N ≥ 10^3 samples gives reasonably good results even far from convergence. Cost is about 0.5% of training.
findings.relevance: Supports the mechanism behind H1.3.6: a ~220-step run with BN momentum ~0.6 and lerped buffers is the regime where EMA stats are least accurate. A 1k–5k image pass is enough, so the cost is well under 0.1 s. Effect size on CIFAR-100 short runs is unknown; the ImageNet gap is an extreme case.

findings.claim: Newton-Schulz uses 3 steps with (a,b,c) = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315) in bf16. Muon renormalizes each filter on every step with p.data.mul_(len(p)**0.5/p.norm()). Batch 2000, 8 epochs, lr 0.24/0.053/0.67, Muon momentum 0.6, SGD momentum 0.85, label smoothing 0.2, BN momentum 0.6, whitening bias trained for 3 epochs, TTA used.
findings.relevance: For H1.5.4: if the port copies this renormalization, filter weight decay is inert and the question is settled by reading the code. For H1.2.3: 3 NS steps is the reference count, so if the port uses 5 the cut is directly supported, and if it uses 3 there is no easy cut left.

findings.claim: Hiverge record (94% CIFAR-10, 1.98 s). Batch 1536, total steps ceil(7.65 × loader length). Muon: lr 0.205, momentum 0.655, 3 NS iterations, momentum buffer in fp16. Filters are renormalized every 2 + int(15·progress) steps toward a target norm shrinking from 0.5012 to 0.0786; wd is 1.04e-6 × batch size. SGD momentum 0.825; lr 0.0573 for biases and 0.5415 for the head. LR decays linearly to 0 with no warm-up. Label smoothing 0.09. Colour jitter: brightness 0.1399, contrast 0.1308. Whitening bias trained for 20% of steps. BN momentum 0.5566, eps 1e-12. TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: Gives concrete untested settings: less frequent renormalization (H1.2.3), shrinking norm target instead of wd (H1.5), LS 0.09 (H1.5.5), colour jitter (H1.5.8), batch 1536 under Muon (H5.1.2), fp16 momentum buffer (less memory traffic), SGD momentum 0.825. Caveat: the record uses TTA (banned here) on a 10-class task, so its label-smoothing and jitter values may not transfer.

findings.claim: 'How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need?' finds training quality is not governed monotonically by how accurately the polar decomposition is computed. A five-step cubic construction uses 10 dominant matmuls versus 15 for five quintic Newton-Schulz iterations, and matches quintic within about 1e-3 validation loss (GPT-2 Small; 1–4B MoE/Mamba). No conv or CIFAR experiments.
findings.relevance: Indirect support for H1.2.3: cheaper or less exact orthogonalization usually keeps quality. Transfer to small conv filters at batch 2000 is unverified.

findings.claim: Polar Express chooses a minimax-optimal quintic polynomial at each iteration. It converges faster than the fixed Newton-Schulz coefficients in both early and late iterations, and improved GPT-2 validation loss inside Muon.
findings.relevance: A way to keep orthogonality while running fewer NS iterations (e.g. 2 instead of 3) if the port already uses 3. This would extend H1.2.3 at near-zero code risk, since only the coefficients change.

findings.claim: Muon critical batch size, tested on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, VGG-16/CIFAR-100 and Llama 160M. Muon needs fewer steps to reach 90% CIFAR-10 test accuracy than AdamW or momentum SGD at every batch size tested, and its sample-efficiency advantage grows at larger batches. Nesterov momentum plus weight decay gives the largest critical batch size among the Muon variants.
findings.relevance: Weak support for H5.1: under Muon, batch can probably move without SGD's penalty. The paper gives no CIFAR-100 optimum for ~220-step airbench runs, so H5.1.1 and H5.1.2 remain empirical.

findings.claim: Seesaw: where a schedule would cut LR by a factor α, cut it by √α and raise the batch by α instead. This matches cosine-decay loss with about 36% fewer serial steps, but only below the critical batch size, in the noise-dominated regime.
findings.relevance: A new direction not in the tree: grow the batch late in the decay phase (e.g. 2000→3000 in the final 32 px phase) so fewer steps carry the fixed per-step cost (~5% overhead plus ~3.8% Muon NS). Expected gain is small (~1–3%) and is at risk if batch 2000 is already above CIFAR-100's critical batch. Related to H5.1.3, which uses the opposite ordering.

findings.claim: FreezeOut on CIFAR-10/100 gives up to about 20% wall-clock savings with no accuracy loss for ResNets/WRNs, about 3% loss for DenseNets, and no gain for VGG. MosaicML's layer-freezing method card reports mixed results on larger benchmarks.
findings.relevance: Matches E028/E034/E036 (the freeze was free) and E037's limit: freezing too early costs accuracy. Further dose gains are probably limited.

findings.claim: The only public submission to the AIDDA CIFAR-100 speedrun is an airbench-based recipe: 75.29% mean (sd 0.25 pp) over 40 trials, 8.11 s (sd 0.02) on a Modal A100-SXM4-80GB, with no TTA and compile plus warm-up in untimed build. The organizer's ResNet9 baseline (40 epochs, width 64) scored 75.36% in 59.30 s on the A100 PCIe. The upstream repo shows no public PRs.
findings.relevance: The loop's tip (~5.3 s, held-out population mean ~0.755) is already about 35% faster than the best public CIFAR-100 recipe. No public CIFAR-100-specific tricks are left to borrow. The 0.25 pp per-seed sd matches H4.1.

findings.claim: airbench96 was evaluated on CIFAR-100 with CIFAR-10 hyperparameters, untuned. It beat ResNet-18 training by 1.7%, with or without Cutout.
findings.relevance: Supports H1.5: the airbench hyperparameters were never tuned for CIFAR-100, consistent with the loop's wd ×0.5 gain (E016). Gives no specific optimum.

findings.claim: The CIFAR-10 record agent's legitimate gains were progressive resizing (24→28→32), pooling changes, CUDA graphs and optimizer fusion. Flagged specification gaming: precomputing augmentation outside the timed region (~0.150 s), moving per-trial whitening and batch preprocessing into untimed setup, a 60 s thermal cooldown (~0.040 s) and selecting faster hosts (~0.009 s).
findings.relevance: A compliance guardrail for H3.2 and H3: moves like warming prepare's kernels on synthetic data (E035) are fine, but anything that computes whitening or augmentation from real data in build is the documented gaming pattern and breaks the rules here.
